title: Bonaventure's mind
hookLine: the Franciscan way of thinking: love goes further than knowledge

lines: A FOUNDER WHO WROTE NO THEOLOGY.
A FRIAR IN A LECTURE HALL.
cards: Francis never wrote a book of theology. He told his brothers to work with their hands, to preach peace, to bear a locked gate patiently. Then the brotherhood grows, and some of the friars end up in lecture halls.

One of them teaches at the university of Paris, in a world of disputations, where a question is argued for and against, point by point. So what does a friar like that do with a founder who preached to birds?
Does he leave the stories behind? Today, the scholar who tried to think the Franciscan way.

teach.h: SIX WINGS, SIX STEPS TO GOD.
teach.b: His name is Bonaventure. He taught in Paris, he led the Franciscan order, and he wrote a life of Francis.
He also wrote a short book with a long name, The Journey of the Mind into God, which this path has walked once before.

He went up to La Verna, the mountain where Francis had seen a vision of a seraph, an angel with six wings, and there, looking for peace, he came to see the six wings as six steps of a journey toward God.
First you find God's traces in the world outside: in stones, plants, birds, everything that is. Then you turn inward and find God's image in your own mind, in memory, understanding and love.
Then you look above the mind, to God himself. It's a ladder of thought, and hard going.
But before you set out, Bonaventure warns: don't think reading is enough without the anointing of grace, or thinking without devotion, or study without wonder, or knowledge without love.
And at the top of the ladder he tells the mind to let go of its thinking.
If you want to know how this happens, ask grace, not learning. Ask desire, not understanding. Ask the groaning of prayer, not the diligence of study.

Ask the Bridegroom, not the teacher. Paul says it to the Corinthians, in the Douay-Rheims: "Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth." Bonaventure didn't throw away knowledge; he spent his life teaching and writing.
But in this book knowledge reaches an edge, and love keeps going.

teach.h: KNOWLEDGE PUFFETH UP; BUT CHARITY EDIFIETH.
teach.b: Think as hard as you can, then let love carry you the rest of the way.

how: Franciscans and other Catholics read Bonaventure's Journey of the Mind into God as a guide to prayer, and the Church honors him as a saint and a Doctor of the Church.

o: a method for memorizing the whole of Scripture
a well-known proof that God exists, built from logic
a ladder of thought toward God that ends in love

s: he taught in Paris and wrote volumes. he warned against knowledge without love, not knowledge.
Bonaventure read the six wings of Francis's seraph as six steps toward God
outside in the world, inside in the mind, then above the mind.
at the top of Bonaventure's ladder, the mind finally understands everything
at the top he tells the mind to let go: ask desire, not understanding.

games.q: you're Bonaventure, at the top of your ladder of thought. how do you say the last step is reached?
o: by asking grace, desire and prayer, not learning.
by arguing it out with a better teacher.
games.why: he tells the mind to ask grace, not learning; desire, not understanding; the Bridegroom, not the teacher.

practice: Bring to mind someone you don't understand, and if part of you wants to solve them first, let that rest; you can stay puzzled. Now, without understanding them any better, wish them well: their health, their peace, their good.
If you pray, hold them before God, puzzle and all.

wordCard.voice: Bonaventure's mind. A scholar's ladder of thought toward God, that ends by letting go of thinking and asking for love. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin: a guide for a journey; the first word of the book's Latin title.

carryVoice: Your line: love goes further. Bonaventure's ladder ends in prayer, not in an answer. That's today, done.

sources.q: Knowledge puffeth up; but charity edifieth.
